question: to the Commission António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Tiago Moreira de Sá (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Dick Erixon (ECR), Petra Steger (PfE), Jacek Ozdoba (ECR), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Hans Neuhoff (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Erik Kaliňák (NI), Petar Volgin (ESN), Roman Haider (PfE), Friedrich Pürner (NI), Susanna Ceccardi (PfE), Milan Uhrík (ESN), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Gerald Hauser (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR), Barbara Bonte (PfE), Gerolf Annemans (PfE), Virginie Joron (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Marc Jongen (ESN), András László (PfE), Dominik Tarczyński (ECR), György Hölvényi (PfE), Kinga Gál (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), András Gyürk (PfE), Csaba Dömötör (PfE), Viktória Ferenc (PfE), Ernő Schaller-Baross (PfE), Enikő Győri (PfE) Subject:

A publication by the US House Judiciary Committee reports that, in the context of Regulation (EU) 2022/20651 (the Digital Services Act – DSA) and related initiatives, Commission contacts with online platforms included requests or recommendations affecting the visibility of lawful political content, including criticism of EU migration policy, critiques of gender ideology and political satire. This raises serious concerns under Article 5(1) and (2) and Article 13(2) of the Treaty on European Union and Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, particularly during electoral periods. The Commission is asked: 1.

In the last 24 months, how many Commission-initiated contacts with platforms and search engines concerned content moderation, ranking/visibility measures (including labelling/downranking) or DSA risk-mitigation?

Can the Commission confirm that it has no competence to monitor lawful public discourse and that, under the Treaties and the DSA, its role is limited to supervising compliance procedures, not shaping the reach or visibility of lawful political opinions?

In the light of Article 15 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and Article 42 of the Charter, when is the Commission going to publish a searchable public register of these contacts (including dates, platforms, Commission services, participants, legal basis, and whether a request/recommendation was made)?

Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act) (OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.5.2026) The Commission rejects the report’s unsubstantiated and unfounded allegations. Freedom of expression is a fundamental right enshrined in the Charter1. The Digital Services Act (DSA)2 protects users by entitling them to explanations, appeals and redress when their content is removed or restricted. Since its application, online platforms have reversed almost 50 million decisions3, demonstrating how the DSA empowers users and effectively protects them against arbitrary platform moderation. The DSA does not prescribe which content is illegal; this is determined purely by national law or other EU laws. The Commission cannot order providers of online services to remove or amend specific content from their services. Platforms remove content based on their own policies. The DSA mandates the largest platforms4 to identify, analyse and assess systemic risks in the EU stemming from their services, and to mitigate those risks. This includes risks to electoral processes. The DSA brings accountability and transparency. For example, it requires providers of online platforms to issue statements of reasons explaining their moderation decisions in a Transparency Database5. Here, providers must specify the reason for restricting or removing content. The DSA requires the Commission and national competent authorities to publish all key enforcement decisions. This is done through a dedicated website6, with due regard to the rights and legitimate interests of providers and to the protection of confidential information concerning other persons involved, in line with established practice amongst all similar regulatory and enforcement frameworks. Moreover, the Commission’s general transparency rules apply to meetings involving Senior Managers.
